Persian is an Iranian language of the Indo-European family, spoken today by over 100 million people, mostly in Iran, Afghanistan, where it is called Dari, and Tajikistan, where it is called Tajik. For a thousand years it was the language of courts and high culture from Anatolia to Bengal.

It has three stages:

  • Old Persian, written in cuneiform in the inscriptions of the Achaemenid kings, such as the Behistun inscription.
  • Middle Persian, or Pahlavi, the language of the Sasanian Empire and its Zoroastrian books.
  • New Persian, written in Arabic script from the 800s, with many Arabic loanwords.

New Persian rose as a written language at the court of the Samanids in Bukhara. Ferdowsi's Shahnameh, finished around 1010, retold Iran's history in a Persian with few Arabic words and helped keep the language alive. Classic poets such as Omar Khayyam, Rumi, Saadi and Hafez followed.

Turkish and Mongol rulers took it up too. In India it was the language of government and letters under the Delhi sultans and the Mughals, the language of the poet Amir Khusrau and of Abul Fazl's history of Akbar. Poets such as Ghalib and Muhammad Iqbal still wrote in it, alongside Urdu, which it shaped deeply. In 1837 the British replaced it in Indian courts and offices with English and local languages.
